model.label: Tax-funded national health service, run by 19 regions and two autonomous provinces within a national benefits package (LEA)

overview.statement: Article 32 of Italy's 1948 Constitution protects health as a fundamental right of the individual and an interest of society, and commits the Republic to free care for people who are indigent.

The National Health Service (SSN) covers every citizen and every foreign national who is ordinarily resident, and coverage is automatic; undocumented migrants are entitled only to urgent and essential care.

locator.section: How much is spent on health services? Coverage

overview.statement: The SSN is a universal, publicly financed service run by 19 regions and two autonomous provinces; the Ministry of Health sets priorities, passes tax revenue to them as block grants, and checks their performance through the New Guarantee System, which monitors delivery of the national benefits package (LEA).

Regional governments plan and deliver care through local health authorities (ASLs), which hold budgets and provide preventive, primary and hospital care; GPs and paediatricians are gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care, and the mix of public and accredited private hospitals differs widely between regions.
Italy set up its national health service (SSN) in 1978, replacing a fragmented social insurance system with a universal, tax-funded service modelled on the UK's NHS.

locator.section: Coverage and Access: Background and History

overview.statement: A 2001 constitutional reform moved more of the financing and delivery of care to the regions, while the national government kept responsibility for the Essential Levels of Care (LEA), the national benefits package.

locator.section: Coverage and Access: Background and History

financing.statement: The first regional tax that funds the SSN is IRAP, an earmarked tax on companies' value added (operating revenues minus costs) and on public-sector salaries; the review gives its standard level as 3.9%, which regions may raise by up to 0.92 points depending on the industry.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: The second regional tax is a regional surcharge on national personal income tax (addizionale IRPEF), which each region sets differently: some use a flat rate, others rates that rise with income.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: Each region's own revenue from these two taxes, plus expected patient co-payments, is compared with its assessed financial need; the national government covers the gap from an equalisation fund financed by national VAT.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: The five special-statute regions (Valle d'Aosta, Trentino-Alto Adige, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Sicily and Sardinia) receive a direct share of national tax revenue and are expected to fund the national benefits package from their own resources.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: National taxes do most of the equalising, but regional taxation is uneven: richer northern regions have larger tax bases and can add to the funding the central government sets, while the poorest southern regions have little room to raise extra money for health care.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: According to the Finance Ministry's 2025 monitoring report, the money set aside each year for the SSN comes from regional taxes (IRAP and the regional income-tax surcharge), the state's share of VAT, the tax shares of the special-statute regions and autonomous provinces, and a fixed amount of the regional services' own revenue.

locator.section: Capitolo 1 (Sezione I), financing of the SSN

financing.statement: The Finance Ministry's 2025 monitoring report states the fixed own revenue of the regional health services counted in SSN funding as just under EUR 2 billion, coming from patient co-payments (tickets) and doctors' private practice inside public hospitals (intramoenia).
Ordinary funding for the SSN was EUR 134.0 billion in 2024, equal to 6.1% of GDP, up from EUR 128.9 billion (6.0% of GDP) in 2023.

locator.table: Tab. 1.1: ordinary SSN financing, current health spending (national accounts) and GDP, 2015-2024 (EUR million); columns are years 2015-2024

financing.statement: On the OECD System of Health Accounts basis, public sources paid for just over 73% of Italy's health spending in 2023, below the EU average of 80%; almost 90% of the remaining 27% was paid directly out of pocket.
In 2023, private sources accounted for nearly 27% of Italy's health spending, seven points above the EU average: out-of-pocket payments made up 24% and voluntary health insurance a further 3%.

Employer-run health funds, which mostly play a supplementary role, covered over 16 million people (27% of the population) in 2023, up from 7 million in 2013, largely because of tax incentives; WHO notes these estimates are uncertain.
The average annual contribution to a health fund was EUR 279 per person in 2021, and health funds held EUR 3.2 billion in resources in 2023.

The government encourages health funds through open enrolment, community-rated premiums and a tax incentive that lets employees deduct contributions to non-profit funds from taxable income; to qualify, a fund must be on the national register and spend at least 30% on services the SSN does not cover.

Commercial voluntary health insurance premiums totalled EUR 4.2 billion in 2023, up from under EUR 3.1 billion in 2019; around EUR 1.2 billion of the 2023 total was sold directly to individuals and the rest through health funds buying cover for their members.

Out-of-pocket health spending can be deducted from personal income tax at up to 19% after a EUR 129.11 threshold per taxpayer; for 2023, the Parliamentary Budget Office estimates the resulting tax refund at about EUR 4.6 billion, against EUR 43.1 billion of private health spending recorded by the Tessera Sanitaria system and EUR 26 billion declared by 22.8 million taxpayers.

In tax year 2023, about EUR 3.2 billion of contributions to health funds and mutuals qualified for tax relief (EUR 3 billion of it to type-B funds that exist only for health benefits); the Parliamentary Budget Office estimates the lost personal income tax at about EUR 1.1 billion, over EUR 1 billion of it from type-B funds.

covered.statement: The SSN guarantees the national benefits package (LEA) throughout the country; regions may offer services beyond it only if they pay for them, and the services included are defined through positive and negative lists.

locator.section: How much is spent on health services? Coverage

covered.statement: Publicly covered services include preventive care, inpatient and outpatient care, maternity and primary care, medicines, mental health care, palliative care, rehabilitation, home visits and assistive devices.

locator.section: The Role of Public Health Insurance

covered.statement: The main coverage gaps are dental and mental health care: dental care is covered only for some groups, such as children under 14, and excludes orthodontic prostheses, while psychotherapy for people whose conditions are not severe, and smoking cessation, are generally unavailable.

locator.section: Box 2 What are the key gaps in coverage?

covered.statement: In 2023, public financing paid for 96% of hospital spending in Italy, above the EU average of 91%, and for 63% of retail medicines spending, slightly above the EU average.

Only 58% of spending on outpatient medical services was publicly financed in 2023, against an EU average of 77%; the 2025 profile links this partly to long waits for specialist visits that push patients to pay for faster private care.

The national benefits package was comprehensively revised in 2017, adding new vaccines, outpatient and diagnostic services, neonatal care and health devices, and a list of rare diseases covered by the SSN.

Italy has no dedicated long-term care insurance; instead a cash allowance (indennita di accompagnamento) is paid to people with severe functional limitations regardless of income, EUR 525 a month in 2022.
In 1978 Italy became the first country in Europe to close its mental hospitals, about 100 at the time, and to abolish compulsory treatment of psychiatric patients.

cost_sharing.statement: Primary care and inpatient care are free at the point of use for everyone; services that do carry charges have exemption categories (for example by age or income), but there is no overall annual cap on co-payments.

For outpatient specialist visits, diagnostic tests and dental care, each region sets a fixed co-payment (the 'ticket') per visit or test, ranging from a few cents to about EUR 36; for some specialties one co-payment covers up to eight interventions in the same area.
Patients who go to a specialist without a GP referral pay the full price out of pocket.

Twelve of the 21 regional health services charge fixed co-payments on outpatient prescription medicines, from EUR 2-4 per item to EUR 5-10 per prescription, with exemptions for some groups; the other nine charge none.
Every region applies reference pricing to reimbursable (class A) medicines, which WHO calls a source of 'avoidable co-payments'; the reference price must be at least 20% below the originator's price.

For outpatient specialist visits, income-based exemptions in all regions cover children under 6 and people over 65 in households with gross income under EUR 36,152, and unemployed people and pensioners over 60 in low-income households (under EUR 8,263 for a single person, up to EUR 12,910 with three or more children).

cost_sharing.statement: Emergency department visits judged appropriate at triage are free, as is emergency transport; visits judged inappropriate cost EUR 25 plus a variable fixed charge for the care given (from under EUR 1 to EUR 36).

locator.table: Table 3. User charges for publicly financed health care, 2025: emergency care

cost_sharing.statement: Formal co-payments within the SSN are a small part of out-of-pocket spending: in 2023 the 'ticket' on specialist care and medicines made up only 7.4% of it (EUR 1.71 billion for specialist services and EUR 1.48 billion for medicines), and exemptions covered about 28% of specialist outpatient services delivered.
The 'superticket', a fixed EUR 10 surcharge on most outpatient consultations and diagnostic tests, was abolished in 2020, and the role of formal cost sharing has changed little since.

Out-of-pocket spending on retail medicines was EUR 10.6 billion in 2023, nearly 28% of pharmaceutical spending; it included about EUR 7.1 billion for non-reimbursed class C medicines and EUR 1.1 billion paid by patients who chose an originator over a reimbursed generic, a cost that was higher per person in the South (EUR 23.5) than in the North (EUR 13.3).

financial_hardship.statement: The 2024 health system summary says the SSN cannot always protect people from financial hardship, and that long waiting times are one reason people spend their savings or go into debt to pay for private care.

A 2017 estimate by RBM-CENSIS, cited in the 2022 review, put at nearly 8 million the number of people who, because of excessive waiting times, used all their savings on private care or borrowed to pay for health care, and at 1.8 million those pushed below the poverty line by health expenses.

Catastrophic health spending is heavily concentrated among low-income households: in 2022 it affected 27% of households in the poorest consumption quintile, and it was also above average in households headed by economically inactive, unemployed or retired people, older people living alone, households in the South and those with two or more children.
WHO finds that catastrophic health spending in Italy is driven mainly by outpatient medicines and outpatient care in poorer households and by dental care in richer ones.
Households in the lowest income quintile accounted for 60% of all catastrophic health spending in Italy in 2022.

additional_care.statement: Voluntary health insurance plays a minor, mainly supplementary role (faster treatment and more choice of provider), with a smaller complementary role covering co-payments and excluded services; it made up 2% of current health spending in 2023 and is sold by non-profit health funds and commercial insurers.
Health fund benefits are generally modest: some specialist outpatient care, diagnostic imaging and preventive dental care, with medicines rarely covered.
Under 'intramoenia', hospital doctors see patients privately outside their normal working hours, using the hospital's outpatient and diagnostic facilities, and the patient pays them.

Covered inpatient care has no user charges; extra billing for better accommodation applied to 0.5% of hospital admissions in 2019 and for choosing one's physician to 0.3%, with amounts varying by region and provider.

additional_care.statement: Registered health funds, which receive tax relief, grew from 267 to 324 between 2010 and 2023 and their members from 5.8 to 16.3 million between 2013 and 2023; in the latest year they paid out over EUR 3 billion, almost two thirds of it for services that substitute for, rather than add to, those the SSN guarantees.
